H1.text: Aarav draws a rectangle, four centimetres wide and three tall. Its width grows two centimetres every second. Its height grows three centimetres every second.

H2.text: So does the area grow by two times three, six square centimetres every second?

H3.text: Aarav tested this at his study table tonight.

H4.text: The real answer is much bigger, and it keeps changing. So what went wrong?

H5.text: Today we learn the algebra of derivatives: the derivative of a sum, a product and a fraction.

S1.text: Quick reminder. A derivative tells us how fast something changes. We write u dash for how fast u changes.

S2.text: Start easy. Two tanks fill with water at the same time. One gains two litres a minute, the other three. Together, five litres a minute.

S3.text: That is the sum rule. The derivative of u plus v is u dash plus v dash. For a difference, use a minus.

S4.text: A fixed number in front just comes along. The derivative of five times u is five times u dash.

S5.text: One more tool from the NCERT book. The derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus one. So x cubed gives three x squared.

P1.text: Now the product. Let the rectangle have width u and height v. Its area is u times v.

P2.text: In a tiny moment, the width grows by a small bit, delta u. The height grows by delta v.

P3.text: Watch the new area appear. A strip along the top, u times delta v. A strip down the side, v times delta u.

P4.text: And one tiny corner, delta u times delta v. As the moment shrinks to zero, this corner shrinks much faster, and vanishes.

P5.text: So the area grows at u times v dash, plus v times u dash. Not u dash times v dash.

D1.text: Let us turn the picture into a rule, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. The new area is u delta v, plus v delta u, plus delta u delta v.

D3.text: Step two. Divide by the small time, delta t. Each piece now tells us how fast it grows.

D4.text: Step three. Let delta t go to zero. The corner piece goes to zero too, because it is small times small.

D5.text: Step four. The derivative of u v is u dash v, plus u v dash. NCERT calls this the Leibnitz rule, or the product rule.

D6.text: Back to Aarav. Width four, height three. Four times three, plus three times two, is eighteen. Not six.

R1.text: Now the fraction, u over v. Think of sharing a pizza. More pizza helps each person. More people hurts.

R2.text: So the top's change counts as plus, and the bottom's change counts as minus. The rule is u dash v, minus u v dash, all over v squared.

R3.text: It works only when v is not zero, because we can never divide by zero.

R4.text: A memory trick. Low d high, minus high d low, over the square of what is below.

C1.text: Side by side. For a sum, the derivatives just add. u plus v gives u dash plus v dash.

C2.text: For a product, they do not multiply. Each part takes a turn to change, while the other stays still.

C3.text: Your turn. Is the derivative of x squared times x cubed equal to two x times three x squared? Pause and think.

C4.text: No! That gives six x cubed. The product is x to the power five, so the derivative is five x to the power four. The product rule agrees: two x times x cubed, plus x squared times three x squared.

T1.text: Remember this. A product does not give the product of derivatives. Each part takes a turn.

W2.text: Find the derivative of x squared, over x plus one. Then find its value at x equal to one.

W3.text: Step one. The top u is x squared, so u dash is two x. The bottom v is x plus one, so v dash is one.

W4.text: Step two. Use low d high, minus high d low, over the bottom squared.

W5.text: Step three. That is two x times x plus one, minus x squared, all over x plus one, squared.

W6.text: Step four. Tidy the top. We get x squared plus two x, over x plus one, squared.

W7.text: Step five. At x equal to one, that is three over four. A tiny step of one thousandth on the graph gives the same slope.

X2.text: In the quotient rule, many students start with u v dash. The order flips the sign.

X3.text: For our example, the wrong order gives minus three over four. But the graph is going up at x equal to one, so the slope must be positive. Always start with the bottom times the top's change.

J1.text: Where is this asked? These rules are tools. Exam questions use them as one step inside a bigger calculus problem.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Use the product rule, then the quotient rule. Pause and solve.

A2.text: First, f of one is one times g of one, which is two.

A3.text: By the product rule, f dash of one is g of one, plus one times g dash of one. That is two plus three, which is five.

A4.text: By the quotient rule, h dash of one is five times two, minus two times one, over two squared. Eight over four is two.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is the derivative of a product not the product of the derivatives?

Y3.text: Two. Find the derivative of x plus one, times x plus two.

Y4.text: Three. In the quotient rule, which term comes first on top?
